exercises.prompt: Implement firstEven(arr) so it returns the first even number in arr, or undefined when arr contains no even number. Use Array.prototype.find. firstEven([1, 3, 4, 5]) is 4. An empty array returns undefined.
hints: find scans for the first element that passes a test and hands back that element.
The test for even is x => x % 2 === 0.
return arr.find(x => x % 2 === 0) — find already returns undefined when nothing matches, including for an empty array.

exercises.prompt: Implement hasNegative(arr) so it returns true when arr contains at least one negative number, and false otherwise. Use Array.prototype.some. An empty array returns false.
hints: some asks whether at least one element passes a test, returning a boolean.
Negative means x < 0; hand that test to some.
return arr.some(x => x < 0) — some is false for an empty array, since no element is there to pass.

exercises.prompt: Implement allPositive(arr) so it returns true when every number in arr is strictly greater than zero, and false otherwise. Use Array.prototype.every. An empty array returns true, since there is no element to break the rule.
hints: every returns true only when all elements pass its test — the mirror image of some.
Positive means x > 0; give that test to every.
return arr.every(x => x > 0) — every is true for an empty array, because there is nothing that fails.

exercises.prompt: Implement includesValue(arr, target) so it returns true when target is present in arr and false otherwise, using Array.prototype.includes. An empty array returns false.
hints: includes answers a single yes/no question: is this value somewhere in the array?
It takes the value itself, not a test function: arr.includes(target).
return arr.includes(target) — true when present, false otherwise, and false for an empty array.

exercises.prompt: Implement indexOfValue(arr, target) so it returns the index of the first element strictly equal to target, or -1 when target is not present. Use Array.prototype.indexOf. indexOfValue([3, 1, 4], 1) is 1. An empty array returns -1.
hints: indexOf reports the position of a value, not the value itself.
It returns the index of the first match, or -1 when the value is absent: arr.indexOf(target).
return arr.indexOf(target) — a miss is -1, and the first of several equal values wins.

exercises.prompt: Implement firstIndexAbove(arr, n) so it returns the index of the first element strictly greater than n, or -1 when no element exceeds n. Use Array.prototype.findIndex. firstIndexAbove([1, 5, 3], 4) is 1. An empty array returns -1.
hints: findIndex is like find, but returns the position of the first passing element instead of the element.
The test is a comparison to n: x => x > n.
return arr.findIndex(x => x > n) — strictly greater, and -1 when nothing qualifies.
